passage:
Under the Treaties, the common commercial policy is an exclusive competence of the European Union: in principle, only the Union may legislate and conclude binding agreements on trade in goods and services, the commercial aspects of intellectual property and foreign direct investment. The Commission negotiates trade agreements on the basis of directives adopted by the Council, keeps the European Parliament informed throughout, and presents the outcome for signature and conclusion. The Council then decides, usually by qualified majority, and the Parliament must give its consent.

For many years, however, agreements were concluded as 'mixed' agreements, signed by both the Union and its Member States, because they also covered matters on which competence was shared. A mixed agreement must be ratified by every Member State according to its own procedures, which may involve national and even regional parliaments, so its full entry into force can take many years. In 2017 the Court of Justice, asked for an opinion on the agreement negotiated with Singapore, found that most of its content fell within the Union's exclusive competence, but that the rules on portfolio investment and on the settlement of disputes between investors and states did not.

After that opinion, the Union began to split such deals in two: a trade agreement that it can conclude alone, and a separate investment protection agreement that remains mixed.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Since the 2017 opinion, investment protection agreements no longer need ratification by national parliaments.
After a split, the trade agreement needs no ratification by each Member State to enter into force.
The Court's opinion on the agreement negotiated with Singapore was requested by the European Commission.
The Council always decides by qualified majority when it concludes a trade agreement with a third country.

Turkey has formed a customs union with the European Union since the end of 1995. Industrial goods and processed agricultural products move between the two sides without customs duties, and Turkey applies the Union's common external tariff to imports of these goods from the rest of the world. Services, public procurement and most unprocessed agricultural products are not covered, although some farm goods benefit from separate preferential arrangements.

Turkish officials have long criticised an asymmetry in this arrangement. When the Union concludes a free trade agreement, its partner lowers its duties on EU goods, while goods from that partner that enter the EU at preferential rates can, in principle, then circulate freely into Turkey. Yet the partner has no obligation to open its own market to Turkish goods, because Turkey is not a party to the EU's agreement and must negotiate a separate one, which some partners have been reluctant to conclude. Turkey also has no vote when the Union decides its trade policy, even though it must follow the resulting tariffs.

In 2016 the Commission proposed opening negotiations to modernise the customs union and extend it to services, public procurement and more agricultural products. The Council did not give it a mandate to negotiate, mainly for reasons linked to the wider political relationship, including concerns about democracy and the rule of law in Turkey.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Political tensions were the sole reason why the Council withheld the mandate the Commission sought.
The customs union was conceived from the start as a step towards Turkey's eventual accession to the Union.
Turkish officials would prefer to replace the customs union with a free trade agreement with the EU.
A Turkish exporter can face duties in an EU trade partner's market that EU exporters there avoid.

Dumping occurs when a company exports a product at a price below its 'normal value', which is generally the price charged for the same product on the exporter's home market. The rules of the World Trade Organization do not prohibit dumping as such, but they allow an importing country to impose anti-dumping duties when dumped imports cause material injury to its own industry.

In the European Union, the Commission normally opens an investigation after receiving a complaint from, or on behalf of, EU producers. Before imposing duties, it must establish four things: that the imports are dumped, that the EU industry has suffered material injury, that the dumped imports caused that injury, and that measures would not be against the interest of the Union as a whole, an assessment that also takes account of importers and users. Provisional duties may be imposed during the investigation, which must be completed within 14 months at the latest.

Definitive duties normally apply for five years and can be extended following an expiry review. Under the 'lesser duty rule', the duty is set below the full dumping margin when a lower rate would be enough to remove the injury, although since 2018 the Union may set this rule aside, for example when raw material prices in the exporting country are distorted.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Proof of dumping and of harm to EU producers is not, by itself, enough to justify duties.
Definitive duties remain in force indefinitely unless the exporter concerned raises its export prices.
Anti-dumping duties are likely to raise the prices paid by EU consumers of the product.
Since 2018, the Union has always set the lesser duty rule aside when raw material prices are distorted.

The anti-coercion instrument, which entered into force at the end of 2023, is meant to deter third countries from using trade or investment measures to pressure the European Union or a Member State into making a particular policy choice. Such pressure may take formal shapes, such as tariffs or import bans, or informal ones, such as sudden boycotts or unexplained obstacles at the border.

The procedure has several stages. The Commission first examines a possible case, either on its own initiative or on the basis of information it receives. If it concludes that coercion is taking place, it proposes that the Council confirm this finding. The Council decides by qualified majority, so a single government cannot block the determination. The Union then tries to end the coercion through engagement with the country concerned, for instance by negotiation, mediation or international adjudication. Only if this fails may the Commission adopt response measures, such as duties or restrictions on trade in services or on access to public procurement, and these must not exceed the level of injury suffered by the Union.

Supporters regard the instrument chiefly as a deterrent: the hope is that its mere existence will make its use unnecessary. Critics fear that it could invite retaliation, or that it will be hard to activate because governments may hesitate to confront a major trading partner.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Coercion covers any measure taken by a third country that affects its trade with the Union.
The instrument was probably adopted in response to Chinese trade restrictions on Lithuania.
A lone government objecting to a finding of coercion is unable to block it in the Council.
Critics are certain that any use of the instrument will lead third countries to retaliate.

The European External Action Service (EEAS), which began work in January 2011, is the European Union's diplomatic service. It was created by the Treaty of Lisbon to support the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, who conducts the common foreign and security policy, chairs the Foreign Affairs Council and is at the same time a Vice-President of the Commission. This 'double hat' was meant to bring together the intergovernmental side of foreign policy, run by the Member States in the Council, and the Union's external instruments, such as trade and development aid, which are managed largely by the Commission.

The EEAS is neither a Commission department nor part of the Council's secretariat but a functionally autonomous body. Its staff come from three sources: officials of the Commission, officials of the Council's General Secretariat, and diplomats seconded from national foreign ministries, who are meant to make up at least a third of its staff at policy level. It runs a network of more than 140 EU delegations around the world, which represent the Union as a whole.

The service does not replace national embassies, which continue to defend the interests of their own countries, but EU delegations increasingly coordinate the work of Member States' missions on the ground.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The running costs of the service are paid mainly by the national foreign ministries.
The High Representative is appointed by the European Council with the Commission President's agreement.
Diplomats from national ministries are expected to fill a minimum share of its policy-level posts.
EU delegations now coordinate all the work of Member States' embassies in every country.

Decisions under the common foreign and security policy are, as a rule, taken unanimously by the Council or the European Council, which gives each Member State a veto. The Treaty softens this rule in two ways. First, abstention does not prevent a unanimous decision, and a government may qualify its abstention with a formal declaration. This 'constructive abstention' frees it from the obligation to apply the decision, but it must accept that the decision commits the Union and refrain from any action likely to conflict with it. If the members abstaining in this way represent at least one third of the Member States comprising at least one third of the Union's population, the decision is not adopted.

Second, the Treaty lists cases in which the Council acts by qualified majority, for instance when it adopts a decision implementing a strategy already agreed unanimously by the European Council, or when it appoints a special representative. Even then, a government that declares vital and stated reasons of national policy can prevent the vote from being taken, and decisions with military or defence implications are always excluded from majority voting.

Several governments have argued for extending majority voting to more areas of foreign policy, but others, often smaller states, fear being outvoted on questions they regard as vital.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Decisions with military implications never go to a majority vote, even to implement an agreed strategy.
A Member State that abstains constructively must still apply the decision on its own national territory.
Majority voting is likely to be extended to decisions on sanctions within the next few years.
Constructive abstention by states with a third of the Union's population is enough to stop a decision.

passage:
Restrictive measures, commonly called sanctions, are among the Union's main foreign policy tools. They can target governments, companies, groups or individuals, and include arms embargoes, travel bans, asset freezes and restrictions on trade in particular goods. Their stated aim is not to punish but to bring about a change in policy or conduct, and they are meant to be targeted so as to limit their impact on the wider population.

Adopting them involves two steps. The Council first adopts a decision under the common foreign and security policy, which requires unanimity. Where the measures fall within the Union's competences, for instance an asset freeze or a trade restriction, the Council then adopts a regulation by qualified majority, on a joint proposal from the High Representative and the Commission. Travel bans, by contrast, are implemented by the Member States themselves. National authorities are also responsible for enforcement and for setting penalties, and a directive adopted in 2024 requires them to make intentional breaches criminal offences.

Listed persons can challenge their designation before the General Court, even though the Court of Justice otherwise has very limited jurisdiction in foreign policy. The courts have annulled a number of listings because the Council could not show sufficient evidence to support the reasons it had given.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The courts annul a listing whenever the person concerned disputes the reasons given by the Council.
The Union adopts restrictive measures only after the UN Security Council has adopted similar ones.
Restrictive measures are designed so that they have no effect at all on the wider population.
An asset freeze requires one unanimous Council act and a second one adopted by qualified majority.

passage:
Development cooperation is an area in which the European Union and its Member States share competence in a particular way: the Union can conduct its own policy and fund its own programmes, but this does not prevent the Member States from pursuing theirs. The Treaty states that the primary objective of Union development policy is the reduction and, in the long term, the eradication of poverty. It also requires the Union to take account of development objectives in those of its other policies that are likely to affect developing countries, a principle known as policy coherence for development.

Much EU funding for partner countries in 2021–2027 is channelled through the Union's largest external instrument, known as Global Europe, which merged several earlier instruments and brought the European Development Fund, previously financed outside the budget by direct national contributions, into the EU budget. Taken together, the Union and its Member States are the world's largest provider of official development assistance, and they have committed to raising it collectively to 0.7% of gross national income by 2030.

Progress towards that target is uneven. A few Member States already meet or exceed it, while others give far less, and several governments have recently cut their aid budgets in favour of defence or domestic priorities.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The European Development Fund is still financed outside the EU budget by national contributions.
An EU-funded programme in a partner country does not stop a Member State from running its own there.
Global Europe also pays for emergency humanitarian aid after natural disasters in partner countries.
The Treaty requires all EU policies to be designed chiefly to reduce poverty in developing countries.

The European Union, together with its Member States, is one of the world's leading donors of humanitarian aid. Within the Commission, this work is managed by the Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations, still widely known by its former acronym, ECHO. The Commission does not deliver most of the aid itself: it funds around 200 partner organisations, including United Nations agencies, the Red Cross and Red Crescent movement and non-governmental organisations, while its field experts monitor how the money is spent.

EU humanitarian aid is bound by four principles: humanity, neutrality, impartiality and independence. Impartiality means that aid is allocated solely on the basis of need, without discrimination between or within affected populations; independence means that humanitarian objectives must remain separate from political, economic or military ones. For this reason the Union insists that humanitarian aid is not a crisis-management tool, even when it is delivered in the same places as its diplomatic or military missions.

These principles can be difficult to apply. Agencies need the consent of those who control a territory to reach people in need, and armed groups or governments often impose conditions or obstruct access. Donors are also criticised for paying more attention to crises that attract media coverage than to protracted, 'forgotten' emergencies.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Donors pay attention only to those crises that attract coverage in the media.
ECHO usually reserves a fixed share of its annual budget for protracted, 'forgotten' crises.
Armed groups and governments always obstruct the delivery of humanitarian aid to people in need.
A community politically close to the EU should get no more aid than its needs justify.

When a disaster overwhelms a country's capacity to respond, its government can ask for help through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism. Created in 2001, the Mechanism includes all Member States and several non-EU participating states, but requests for assistance may come from any country in the world, as well as from the United Nations and some other international organisations. Requests are received by the Emergency Response Coordination Centre in Brussels, which operates around the clock and passes them on to the participating states. Each of them decides voluntarily whether to offer teams, equipment or expertise, and the Union can co-finance the cost of transporting them.

To make help more predictable, participating states can pre-commit resources to a European Civil Protection Pool. In 2019 the Union added a further layer, rescEU, a reserve that includes firefighting aircraft and helicopters, medical stockpiles and equipment for chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear emergencies. These capacities are hosted by participating states but financed largely or entirely from the EU budget, and they are deployed as a last resort when other means are insufficient.

The Mechanism has been activated for floods, wildfires, earthquakes and pandemics, as well as for the war in Ukraine. Its heavy use during summer wildfire seasons has led the Union to expand the firefighting capacity of rescEU.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Ukraine joined the Mechanism as a participating state after the full-scale Russian invasion of 2022.
Every participating state is free to refuse a request for help, whichever country has made it.
Requests from United Nations agencies are handled by a separate coordination centre in Geneva.
All of the costs of the rescEU capacities hosted by participating states are paid from the EU budget.

The European Neighbourhood Policy was launched in 2004, the year of the Union's largest enlargement, to build closer relations with the countries to its east and south without offering them membership. It covers sixteen partners: ten in North Africa and the Middle East, and six in Eastern Europe and the South Caucasus, which since 2009 have also been grouped in the Eastern Partnership. Russia chose not to take part and pursued a separate relationship with the Union.

The policy offers partners closer trade ties, financial support and cooperation in areas such as energy, migration and education, in exchange for political and economic reforms. After the Arab uprisings of 2011, the Union restated this as a 'more for more' approach: partners that reform faster should receive more support. In practice, critics argue, the leverage was limited, since the most attractive incentive, a membership perspective, was not on offer, and the Union often gave priority to stability and migration control over reform.

The line between neighbourhood and enlargement has since blurred. Ukraine and Moldova were granted candidate status in 2022, and Georgia in 2023, so three eastern partners now have the membership perspective that the policy originally withheld. Belarus, by contrast, suspended its participation in the Eastern Partnership in 2021.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Under 'more for more', a slow reformer should receive less EU support than a faster one.
Southern partners have received a larger share of neighbourhood funding than eastern ones.
Critics say the Union always put stability and migration control ahead of reform in its neighbourhood.
Every eastern partner now has the membership perspective the policy originally withheld.

Global Gateway, presented by the European Commission in December 2021, is the European Union's strategy for investment in infrastructure in partner countries. It set out to mobilise up to €300 billion between 2021 and 2027 for projects in five areas: digital networks, climate and energy, transport, health, and education and research. It is widely seen as a European answer to China's Belt and Road Initiative, although EU officials prefer to present it as a values-based offer, stressing transparency, high environmental and social standards and the avoidance of unsustainable debt.

The headline figure needs careful reading. Only a limited part of it consists of EU grants. Much of the amount is expected to come from loans by European development finance institutions, including the European Investment Bank, and from private investors attracted by EU budget guarantees, which cover part of the risk of projects that might otherwise be considered too risky. The strategy is delivered through a 'Team Europe' approach that pools resources from the Union, its Member States and their financial institutions.

Critics argue that many projects listed under the brand were planned before 2021, and that the private capital it claims to mobilise is hard to verify. Supporters reply that the label has helped to coordinate European offers and made them more visible to partner governments.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: EU budget guarantees remove the risk of the projects for private investors.
The European Investment Bank is likely to provide the largest single share of the finance.
The €300 billion figure is not an amount that the Union itself will hand out as grants.
Critics claim that none of the projects under the brand is genuinely new.

Under its common security and defence policy, the European Union deploys civilian missions and military operations outside its territory for tasks such as crisis management, conflict prevention, the training of security forces and the monitoring of ceasefires. They are launched by a unanimous decision of the Council. The Union has no army of its own: personnel and equipment are provided by the Member States and, in some cases, by partner countries.

Funding follows a distinction made in the Treaty. The running costs of civilian missions are paid from the EU budget, whereas expenditure arising from operations with military or defence implications cannot be charged to it. Common costs of military operations, such as their headquarters, are therefore financed by contributions from the Member States, today through the European Peace Facility, while each country pays for the troops and equipment it sends. Most costs thus 'lie where they fall'.

The naval operation Atalanta, launched off the coast of Somalia in 2008, is one of the Union's longest-running military operations. It was set up to protect vessels of the World Food Programme and to deter piracy, and its tasks have since been widened. In 2024 the Union launched another naval operation, Aspides, to protect merchant shipping in the Red Sea; its mandate is defensive, so it does not strike targets on land.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The EU budget never pays the headquarters costs of an EU naval operation.
Civilian missions are financed by contributions from the Member States through the European Peace Facility.
Operation Atalanta has almost eliminated piracy off the coast of Somalia since its launch in 2008.
All the costs of an EU military operation lie where they fall, with the countries taking part.

passage:
The European Peace Facility, set up in 2021, is an off-budget fund through which the European Union finances action in the field of security and defence. Because the Treaty prevents military expenditure from being charged to the EU budget, the Facility is fed by annual contributions from the Member States, calculated according to the size of their economies. It replaced two earlier arrangements: one covering the common costs of the Union's military operations, and another supporting peace operations led by the African Union.

Its main novelty was to allow the Union, for the first time, to finance military equipment for the armed forces of partner countries, including lethal weapons. This became central after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, when the Facility was used to reimburse Member States for weapons and ammunition they had delivered to Ukraine. Its financial ceiling has been raised several times as a result.

Decisions on assistance measures require unanimity in the Council. To accommodate militarily neutral states, a Member State may abstain constructively: it then does not pay towards lethal equipment and contributes instead to other, non-lethal measures. Even so, a single government can delay or block new tranches of support, which happened repeatedly from 2023 onward.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The Facility finances lethal weapons for the armed forces of every partner country that it supports.
It was the Hungarian government that delayed or blocked new tranches for Ukraine from 2023 onward.
The Facility also finances humanitarian aid for civilians caught up in conflict zones.
A Member State that abstains constructively still contributes financially to the Facility.

In March 2022, a few weeks after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Council approved the Strategic Compass, a plan to strengthen the European Union's security and defence policy by 2030. Work on it had begun in 2020 with the first common analysis of the threats facing the Union, prepared with input from national intelligence services. The document is organised around four strands of action: act, secure, invest and partner.

Its best-known commitment is a Rapid Deployment Capacity, a force of up to 5,000 troops able to deploy quickly in a crisis, which was meant to be ready by 2025. Unlike the earlier EU battlegroups, which were never used, the new capacity is designed to be modular, combining land, air and maritime components according to the mission. The Compass also called for regular live exercises, better military mobility, stronger defences against cyber-attacks and disinformation, and more spending on defence capabilities.

The Compass does not create a European army, and it states that NATO remains the foundation of collective defence for its members. Its implementation depends largely on the Member States, which control the forces and budgets involved, and the High Representative reports on progress every year.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The first mission of the Rapid Deployment Capacity took place in 2025, as originally planned.
The new rapid force was designed to be more flexible in make-up than the old battlegroups.
The common threat analysis was published in full so that citizens could read it.
Implementation of the Compass depends entirely on the Member States and the forces they control.

Through its Generalised Scheme of Preferences, the European Union lowers or removes import duties on goods from developing countries without asking for reciprocal concessions. The scheme has three tiers. The standard arrangement reduces duties on about two thirds of tariff lines for low and lower-middle-income countries. A second tier, known as GSP+, removes duties on the same lines for vulnerable countries that ratify and effectively implement 27 international conventions on human and labour rights, the environment and good governance. The third, 'Everything But Arms', grants the least developed countries duty-free and quota-free access for all products except arms and ammunition.

Preferences can be withdrawn, temporarily and wholly or in part, if a beneficiary commits serious and systematic violations of the principles of core human and labour rights conventions. This has happened rarely; in 2020, for instance, the Union suspended part of Cambodia's preferences. A country also leaves the standard arrangement and GSP+ once the World Bank has classified it as an upper-middle-income country for three consecutive years, whereas least developed countries keep Everything But Arms until the United Nations removes them from its list of such countries, after which a transition period applies.

The scheme thus differs from a free trade agreement, which opens markets on both sides.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The partial suspension of Cambodia's preferences mainly affected garments and footwear.
GSP+ beneficiaries must lower their own duties on EU goods in return for their preferences.
Rising income alone does not cost a least developed country its Everything But Arms access.
Everything But Arms removes duties on all goods from developing countries except weapons.

passage:
Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union provides that if a Member State is the victim of armed aggression on its territory, the other Member States have an obligation of aid and assistance towards it by all the means in their power. The clause adds two qualifications. It does not prejudice the specific character of the security and defence policy of certain Member States, a phrase usually understood to protect neutral or militarily non-aligned countries. And commitments in this area must be consistent with those made in NATO, which remains the foundation of collective defence for the states that belong to it.

The clause was invoked for the first time by France after the terrorist attacks in Paris in November 2015. Other Member States responded in different ways, for example by contributing to operations abroad and so relieving French forces. The episode showed that the clause prescribes no procedure and no particular role for the EU institutions: it works mainly between governments.

It should not be confused with the solidarity clause in Article 222 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which applies when a Member State suffers a terrorist attack or a natural or man-made disaster, and which explicitly involves the Union's own instruments.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The clause obliges every Member State to send military help to a state under armed attack.
Neutral Member States declined to offer France any help after the attacks of 2015.
The clause was probably drafted to reassure the Member States that are not in NATO.
Unlike the solidarity clause, Article 42(7) works mainly between governments.

In 1817 the economist David Ricardo set out the principle of comparative advantage with a now famous example. He supposed that Portugal could produce both wine and cloth with less labour than England. Even so, he argued, both countries would gain from trade if each specialised in the good it produced at the lowest relative cost, the one in which its advantage was greatest or its disadvantage smallest, and imported the other. What matters is not whether a country is better at producing something in absolute terms, but what it gives up by producing it instead of something else: its opportunity cost.

The insight remains a cornerstone of trade theory because it shows that even a country that is less productive in every sector can take part profitably in international trade, and that the more productive country also gains from doing so.

The model rests on simplifying assumptions, however. It assumes that workers can move freely between sectors within a country, that there is full employment and that there are no transport costs. Later economists showed that, when such assumptions do not hold, trade may still raise a country's income overall while leaving particular groups of workers, regions or industries worse off.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Even a country that outperforms its partner in every sector benefits from trading with it.
Ricardo concluded that Portugal should make both wine and cloth, being more efficient at both.
Ricardo's reasoning was later used in Britain to justify the repeal of the Corn Laws.
Later economists found that trade usually leaves particular groups of workers worse off.

For centuries, questions of rank caused bitter disputes between diplomats. Envoys of rival courts quarrelled over who should enter a room first or sit nearest to a monarch, and in 1661 a clash over precedence between the retinues of the Spanish and French ambassadors in London ended in bloodshed. The Congress of Vienna addressed the problem in 1815. Its regulation divided diplomatic agents into classes and provided that, within each class, precedence would depend on the date of the official notification of an envoy's arrival, not on the prestige of the country he represented.

Many of these customs were later codified in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations of 1961, which has been accepted by almost every state. The Convention makes the premises of a mission inviolable: officials of the host state may not enter them without the consent of the head of mission. Diplomatic agents enjoy immunity from the host state's criminal jurisdiction and, with limited exceptions, from its civil jurisdiction.

Immunity is not a licence, however. The sending state can waive it, and the host state may at any time, without giving reasons, declare a diplomat persona non grata, after which the sending state must recall the person or end his or her functions. Because expulsions are often answered by reciprocal expulsions, governments weigh them carefully.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The violent clash of 1661 in London was what directly prompted the rules adopted at Vienna.
After 1815, a small state's envoy could outrank a great power's envoy of the same class.
Expelling a diplomat may damage trade relations between the two states involved.
Diplomats are entirely immune from every kind of legal action brought in the host state.

passage:
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, links the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea and allows ships travelling between Europe and Asia to avoid sailing around Africa. For a voyage between northern Europe and East Asia, the alternative route via the Cape of Good Hope adds several thousand nautical miles and typically one to two weeks of sailing, with higher fuel and crew costs. The canal has no locks, because the sea level is almost the same at both ends.

Its importance makes it vulnerable. In March 2021 the container ship Ever Given ran aground in the canal and blocked it for six days, holding up hundreds of vessels. From late 2023, attacks on merchant ships in the southern Red Sea, near the strait of Bab-el-Mandeb, led many shipping companies to send their vessels around Africa instead. Traffic through the canal fell sharply, cutting Egypt's revenue from transit fees, an important source of foreign currency for the country.

The diversions showed that longer routes are not only a cost for shipowners. Because each voyage takes more time, more ships are needed to maintain the same frequency of service, which reduces the capacity available on the market and can push up freight rates even where demand has not changed.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: During the Red Sea attacks, all shipping companies stopped sending their ships through the canal.
The blockage caused by the Ever Given led to a lasting rise in container freight rates worldwide.
Diverting ships around Africa can raise freight rates even if demand for shipping is unchanged.
Egypt earns its foreign currency mainly from the fees ships pay to use the canal.

The Antarctic Treaty was signed in Washington in 1959 by the twelve countries whose scientists had been active on the continent during the International Geophysical Year of 1957–58, and it entered into force in 1961. Seven of the original signatories had made territorial claims in Antarctica, some of them overlapping. The Treaty did not settle these claims. Instead, it froze them: nothing done while the Treaty is in force can be used to support or deny a claim, and no new claim may be made.

The Treaty reserves Antarctica for peaceful purposes. Military bases, manoeuvres and weapons testing are prohibited, although military personnel and equipment may be used for scientific research or other peaceful ends. Nuclear explosions and the disposal of radioactive waste are banned. To build confidence, observers designated by the Consultative Parties may inspect any station or installation in Antarctica at any time.

More than fifty states are now parties, but decisions are taken by the Consultative Parties, which act by consensus. Besides the original signatories, only states that conduct substantial scientific research in Antarctica can acquire that status. A Protocol on Environmental Protection, signed in Madrid in 1991, designates Antarctica as a natural reserve devoted to peace and science, and prohibits any activity relating to mineral resources other than scientific research.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Under the Treaty, only states with consultative status are able to block a decision.
The Treaty recognised the claims of the seven states that had claimed Antarctic territory.
The United States and the Soviet Union were both among the twelve original signatories.
The Madrid Protocol bans all activity in Antarctica other than scientific research.

passage:
The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), signed in 1947, cut tariffs through successive rounds of negotiations and was built on the principle of non-discrimination. Under the most-favoured-nation rule, an advantage that a member grants to goods from one trading partner must be extended immediately to similar goods from all other members. Customs unions and free trade areas are permitted as an exception, provided they cover substantially all the trade between their members.

The World Trade Organization, which replaced the GATT's institutional framework in 1995, added a stronger system for settling disputes. A panel rules first; either party may then appeal to a standing Appellate Body on questions of law; and reports are adopted unless all members agree to reject them. From December 2019, however, the Appellate Body could no longer hear new appeals, because the United States had blocked the appointment of new members. A losing party could therefore appeal a panel report 'into the void', leaving the dispute unresolved.

In response, the European Union and a number of other members set up a Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement, under which participants agree to settle appeals among themselves through arbitration. It applies only to disputes between members that have joined it.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement restored appeals for every dispute between members.
The United States blocked the appointments because it felt that the Appellate Body had exceeded its mandate.
The GATT removed tariffs between its members altogether through successive negotiating rounds.
A free trade area escapes the most-favoured-nation rule only if it covers substantially all trade within it.
